Wind chill is context, not air temperature

Wind chill estimates how cold exposed skin feels because wind increases heat loss. It is not the actual air temperature and is not used as an input to this heat-balance calculation.

V4 converts the completed exposure’s air movement from m/s to km/h for the Canadian Wind Chill Index. The index is shown at or below 0°C when wind is greater than zero; a low-wind correction is used below 5 km/h. In calm air it is not calculated.

The official index uses wind measured at 10 m. This classroom illustration uses the same slider speed for both calculations without a height correction. It is an approximate comparison, not a meteorological or exposure prediction. The index is displayed without a degree symbol.

V4 follows an illustrative adult through a standardized 60-minute air exposure. It couples a core compartment with a mean skin compartment. Temperature signals drive modelled vasomotion, shivering and sweating; environmental exchange then changes those temperatures. A small change in core temperature can coexist with substantial physiological effort. Heat-budget balance does not establish comfort or sustainable thermoregulation.

1. Model identity, evidence and scope

Framework: Gagge/Pierce two-node thermoregulation, adapted from pythermalcomfort 4.6.0, two_nodes_gagge.py (readable implementation documentation). The exact package version is pinned in verification. The documentation’s “stable” link may change. The code’s coefficient set is the reference for this adaptation; it is not identical to every publication called “Gagge 1986”.

Foundational publication: Gagge, Fobelets & Berglund (1986), A standard predictive index of human response to the thermal environment, ASHRAE Transactions 92(2B), 709–731. The original full text was not available for this build; equations were inspected in the implementation and the primary evaluations linked below. This application does not calculate SET, PMV, comfort or safety categories.

Exploration range: air −20 to 45°C, RH 10–100%, air movement 0–4 m/s, and the four activity settings. This is a software input range, not a validated physiological domain. Subzero exposures are explicitly exploratory. High activity, wind and humidity also extend beyond the selected validation checks. Modelled core temperature is a lumped compartment, not specifically rectal, oesophageal or brain temperature.

Takada, Sakiyama & Matsushita (2011), Tables 1–4 and §3 evaluated sedentary steady-state mean skin temperature; their evidence does not directly validate transient core temperature, shivering or blood flow. Doherty & Arens (1988), model evaluations and Appendix A examined core/skin temperatures and wettedness, finding exercise limitations. Neither establishes accuracy of this adapted model in severe cold.

2. Exposure protocol and variables

Each run begins at core 36.8°C and mean skin 33.7°C, the reference implementation’s initial temperatures. These are a standardized model state, not evidence of equilibrium at 22°C or at the chosen preset. There is no hidden acclimation period. All response variables are recalculated from the initial temperatures. No residual temperature, hydration or response history carries over. The complete exposure is exactly 3,600 simulated seconds.

KindVariables and units
Student inputsAir temperature (°C), relative humidity (%), body-level air movement (m/s), prescribed activity metabolism (W).
Fixed teaching choices70 kg, 1.8 m², 0.5 clo, standing exchange geometry, 101,325 Pa. Mean radiant temperature equals air temperature. No direct sun. External mechanical work = 0.
Evolving statesCore and mean skin temperatures (°C).
Algebraic response variablesModel skin blood flow B (L·m⁻²·h⁻¹), effective skin mass fraction α, shivering (W), sweat secretion (g/h), skin wettedness (dimensionless).
Derived exchangeClothing-surface temperature (°C); core–skin transfer, convection, radiation, skin evaporation, respiration and net storage (whole-body W).

Rest/Light/Moderate/Heavy prescribe 115/230/400/600 W respectively. The labels are illustrative, not universal activity definitions. The conversion is met = W / (1.8 × 58.2), approximately 1.10/2.20/3.82/5.73 met. No external work is subtracted. Shivering is additional. Respiration retains the reference implementation’s activity-only metabolic dependence, and does not increase with shivering. Convection includes the reference’s activity-dependent coefficient.

Changing controls prepares the next exposure; it does not alter displayed results. A reference run is a snapshot of its inputs and history. All endpoint values refer to 60 minutes; the graph shows temperatures throughout. S in watts is an instantaneous rate, not accumulated heat or exposure-averaged storage. Comparisons share scales within each temperature panel. Core and skin panels have separate labelled scales.

3. Heat balances, exchange equations and signs

The following equations use fluxes per square metre. The interface multiplies fluxes by area A = 1.8 m² to show whole-body watts. Exchange is positive outward; negative convection, radiation or respiration is inward heat gain. Internal transfer H is positive from core to skin and cancels from the whole-body budget.

m = m_activity + m_shivering
h_core→skin = (5.28 + 1.163 B)(T_core − T_skin)
s_core = m − h_core→skin − q_res
s_skin = h_core→skin − c − r − e_skin
S = A(s_core + s_skin) = M − C − R − K − E − Q_res

dT_core/dt = A s_core / [c_body mass (1 − α)]
dT_skin/dt = A s_skin / [c_body mass α]
c_body = 0.97 Wh/(kg·K) × 3600 = 3492 J/(kg·K)
α = 0.0417737 + 0.7451833 / (B + 0.585417)

These are effective compartment capacities. Because α changes with blood flow, total stored energy is obtained by integrating S, not by treating mass × c_body × [α T_skin + (1−α) T_core] as a fixed-compartment heat content. Internal tissue conductance is included in H. External contact conduction K is approximated as zero; conduction through clothing is already represented by clothing resistance and is not added again.

v_eff = max(v, 0.1)                     [m/s]
h_c = max(3, 8.600001 v_eff^0.53,
          5.66 (met − 0.85)^0.39)        [W/(m²·K); activity term if met > 0.85]
f_cl = 1 + 0.15 clo;  R_cl = 0.155 clo   [m²·K/W]
h_r = 4 × 0.95 × σ × 0.73 × [(T_cl+T_r)/2 + 273.15]^3
R_a = 1 / [f_cl(h_c + h_r)]
T_cl = (R_a T_skin + R_cl T_air)/(R_a + R_cl)  [T_r = T_air]
c = f_cl h_c(T_cl − T_air)
r = f_cl h_r(T_cl − T_r)

q_res = 0.0023 m_activity(44 − p_air)
      + 0.0014 m_activity(34 − T_air)     [latent + sensible; p in Torr]

The clothing equation is iterated to a 10⁻⁹°C numerical tolerance. The radiation coefficient is the reference’s linearized relation, evaluated at the current clothing and radiant temperatures. It is not V3.2’s quartic implementation. A zero-wind control value still uses 0.1 m/s in physiological exchange, as documented by the reference model. Wind chill uses the supplied speed separately.

Sources: reference kernel: heat-transfer and compartment-update sections; Doherty & Arens, equations 14–35.

4. Vasomotion, shivering, sweat and evaporation

Positive warm/cold signals are departures from the reference core/skin temperatures; negative signals are replaced with zero. These are empirical model response rules. They do not simulate neural pathways, sweat-gland kinetics or all mechanisms of cold defence.

warm_core = max(0, T_core − 36.8); cold_core = max(0, 36.8 − T_core)
warm_skin = max(0, T_skin − 33.7); cold_skin = max(0, 33.7 − T_skin)
B = bound[(6.3 + 120 warm_core)/(1 + 0.5 cold_skin), 0.5, 90]
T_body = α T_skin + (1 − α) T_core
sweat_secretion = min[500, 170 max(0,T_body−36.49) exp(warm_skin/10.7)]
                                                        [g/(m²·h)]
m_shivering = 19.4 cold_skin cold_core                    [W/m²]

B represents model skin blood flow, with L/(m²·h) supported by the dimensional relation using blood heat capacity 1.163 Wh/(L·K). It is not a measured limb flow or a percentage of vasodilation. Sweat units follow 0.68 Wh/g latent heat; the reference documentation’s kg/h/m² label is inconsistent with this conversion. V4 displays g/h for the whole body. The blood and secretion bounds are model parameters, not universal physiological maxima.

Shivering requires both cold signals in this formulation. It has no V3.2 460 W ceiling, no fatigue or exhaustion process and no cold-skin-rate signal. This is a material limitation of cold-response interpretation. Activity may suppress model shivering through its temperature effects, rather than by subtracting activity from a fixed metabolic ceiling.

p_sat(T) = exp[18.6686 − 4030.183/(T+235)]           [Torr]
p_air = RH/100 × p_sat(T_air)
R_e = 1/(2.2 f_cl h_c) + R_cl/(2.2 × 0.45)
e_max = [p_sat(T_skin) − p_air]/R_e                 [W/m²]
w_max = 0.59 v_eff^(−0.08)                         [clothed reference]
e_sweat = min[0.68 × sweat_secretion,
              e_max × max(0,(w_max−0.06)/0.94)]     [for e_max > 0]
e_diffusion = 0.06(e_max − e_sweat)
e_skin = e_sweat + e_diffusion
w = 0.06 + 0.94(e_sweat/e_max)
evaporated_sweat = e_sweat/0.68                    [g/(m²·h)]

Secretion and evaporation remain separate. Fully wet environmental capacity e_max is a potential; the model’s maximum wettedness usually imposes a lower limit. Diffusion is obligatory skin water loss, separate from regulatory sweat. The difference between secreted and evaporated sweat is not a prediction of clothing wetness, retained liquid or runoff. No dehydration history is calculated.

Documented correction: the reference’s saturated branch uses p_rsw = w_max/0.94, inconsistent with its own w = 0.06 + 0.94 p_rsw. V4 uses (w_max−0.06)/0.94 and never evaporates more regulatory sweat than is secreted. At zero capacity evaporation is exactly zero, without a small positive substitute. Negative capacity stops the exposure: condensation heat is outside the represented processes.

Sources: reference response and evaporation branches; Doherty & Arens, equations 25–30 for sweat/diffusion bookkeeping. The correction is algebraic, not a new fitted coefficient.

Adaptations beyond the evaporation correction: controller variables and effective capacities are evaluated consistently at each integration stage. This removes the reference’s one-step lag and arbitrary initial evaporation. At t = 0 the temperatures are unchanged, B = 6.3 and α is derived from B (about 0.150), rather than held at the reference’s first-step 0.1. The mean-body signal reference remains 36.49°C. Endpoint rates are recomputed at the endpoint temperature state.

The reference loop labelled 60 minutes performs 59 one-minute updates; V4 integrates exactly 3600 s and records t = 0. Its smaller-step solver and tighter clothing iteration are numerical adaptations. These differences are isolated in the comparison checks; numerical equality with the original wrapper is not claimed. The app retains no SET/comfort-index calculations or V3.2 compensation rules.

6. Evidence, verification and outstanding limitations

Build checks, 24 September 2026. These results belong to this V4 adaptation, rather than V3.2.

  • Mathematical verification: 1,200 combinations spanning 12 temperatures, five humidities, five wind speeds and four activity levels. 1,080 exposures completed; 120 were explicitly stopped because condensation is not represented; no numerical failures. Maximum instantaneous whole-body balance residual was 3.07e-13 W. Sweat evaporation never exceeded secretion, diffusion remained nonnegative, wettedness limits held, and blood flow remained within the model bounds.
  • Reference implementation: a test-only, unmodified-loop JavaScript port reproduced 12 pythermalcomfort 4.6.0 Python cases across 12 physiological output fields, with maximum absolute difference 2.56e-12 in the native units. This port is only a verification baseline; the shipped V4 includes the documented adaptations.
  • Numerical sensitivity: 10 s, 5 s and 2.5 s integration steps were compared in 12 representative exposures. Halving the shipped 5 s step changed endpoint temperatures by less than 0.000001°C, heat rates by less than 0.001 W, and secretion by less than 0.001 g/h. The largest temperature difference across the recorded histories was less than 0.00002°C. This is numerical convergence, not physiological accuracy.
  • Human-data check: all 56 condition means in Takada et al. Table 1 were compared with the adapted controller. Mean skin-temperature RMSE was 1.12°C, signed bias -0.55°C (model minus observed), and largest absolute difference 2.77°C. No coefficients were fitted. These errors are material and are not individual prediction intervals.

The human-data harness followed Table 3’s comparison assumptions: 81.7 kg, 1.96 m², h_c = 3.1 and h_r = 4.65 W/(m²·K), plus each condition’s clothing and metabolism. It ran for 10 hours to approximate the reported steady-state comparison. The largest terminal skin-temperature drift was 0.014°C/h. These overrides are confined to verification; the student app remains 70 kg, 1.8 m², 0.5 clo and 60 minutes. Several original metabolic rates were estimated, some environmental details were assumed, and the observations are rounded group means. This is a limited reproduction check using a published compilation, not participant-level or independent transient validation.

Outstanding physiological checks: no direct transient human-data validation was completed for this build’s core temperature, sweat secretion, blood flow or shivering. No severe-cold validation was completed. The lower error reported for a different 1986 coefficient set in the paper is not claimed for V4. The 60-minute protocol and changed numerical implementation still need appropriate transient datasets before stronger predictive claims are made.

Application verification: Chromium desktop/laptop, tablet and 390/320 px phone layouts were rendered and inspected. Automated checks covered pending inputs, unchanged displayed artwork, deterministic resets, immutable comparison snapshots, replace/remove actions, keyboard tabs/sliders, dialog closing/focus return, and condensation messaging. No script errors or application network requests occurred during the offline test. Automated WCAG A/AA checks found 0 violations in the tested main view and 0 in the expanded reference dialog. Wide tables are keyboard-focusable. This does not replace a full assistive-technology or cross-browser audit.

Evidence categories: equation checks establish mathematical consistency; reference comparisons establish implementation agreement or quantified differences; human-data checks assess agreement with particular observations. These are distinct. A numerical benchmark or plausible graph is not human-data validation. A published model’s validation does not automatically transfer to V4’s adaptations.

Unsupported processes include regional temperatures and peripheral tissue injury, direct solar radiation, external contact/immersion, wet clothing, hydration dynamics, acclimatization, individual susceptibility, exposure changes during a run, and fatigue or exhaustion of responses. There are no survival, frostbite, hypothermia-countdown or clinical/safety outputs. Temperature outputs are not silently clamped.

Blood-flow bounds, secretion bounds and the absence of a shivering maximum are model assumptions. The selected human checks do not directly establish the accuracy of these variables. Severe-cold and high-activity runs remain exploratory even when numerical convergence is excellent. There are no individual prediction intervals.

7. Wind chill, illustration and accessibility

The Canadian Wind Chill Index remains separate from the engine. For T ≤ 0°C, wind v > 0 and V = 3.6v km/h:

V ≥ 5: WCI = 13.12 + 0.6215T − 11.37V^0.16 + 0.3965TV^0.16
0 < V < 5: WCI = T + [(−1.59 + 0.1345T)/5]V

Calm air and positive temperatures have no index. The index uses the run’s supplied speed as a stand-in for an official 10 m observation, with no height correction, and is displayed without a degree symbol. It is never used as air temperature in the physiological model. Sources: ECCC glossary and ECCC Wind Chill Index.

The approved V5 activity figures and layered treadmill replace the adult illustration. The V4.2 environmental artwork and embedded fonts are retained. Poses and equipment are illustrative only; clothing remains fixed at 0.5 clo. Scenery does not enter the equations. Snow and vegetation are illustrative, not predicted weather or contact heat. Arrow width is 3 + 11√[min(|W|,600)/600] illustration pixels; it is compressed and capped. The number remains the calculated rate. Near-zero displayed flows use neutral dotted lines. Direction labels supplement blue heat loss and orange heat gain.

Temperature traces use labelled core/skin panels, with solid/current and dashed/reference traces and different endpoint symbols. A temperature table provides the graph’s values. Controls support the keyboard; arrow keys switch the two view tabs. Dialogs close with their Close button or Escape. Reduced-motion settings stop animation. All assets are embedded; only source links need the internet. No student responses, identifiers, telemetry or run histories are collected or stored.

8. Sources and software attribution
  1. pythermalcomfort 4.6.0 source. Tartarini & Schiavon (2020), pythermalcomfort: A Python package for thermal comfort research, SoftwareX 12, 100578. Publication. MIT licence; adapted physiological kernel.
  2. Doherty & Arens (1988), Evaluation of the physiological bases of thermal comfort models. Equations and human-data comparison; Appendix A provides experimental conditions.
  3. Takada, Sakiyama & Matsushita (2011), Validity of the two-node model for predicting steady-state skin temperature. Building and Environment 46, 597–604. Parameter-version comparison and sedentary skin-temperature dataset.
  4. Mou and colleagues (2023), comparative thermoregulation-model study. IBPSA proceedings, DOI 10.26868/25222708.2023.1723. A limited 26→36°C transient skin-temperature comparison; not validation of this build.
  5. Fiala, Lomas & Stohrer (2001) and JOS-3 author repository: alternatives considered during model selection; not sources of borrowed controller coefficients.
